faq.q: Why does a submarine need a periscope?
faq.a: Submarines cannot see out from under water, and windows would be weak spots in the hull. A periscope lets the crew look around above the surface while the submarine stays hidden below.
asks: How do submarines see where they are going?

faq.q: Why is the top mirror at 45 degrees?
faq.a: A mirror at 45 degrees reflects light through exactly 90 degrees, turning light travelling level into light travelling straight down the tube.

faq.q: Why does a periscope have lenses?
faq.a: Without lenses the view down a long thin tube would be tiny. Lenses relay the image down the tube and can magnify it, so distant ships look closer.

faq.q: Why is the periscope view the right way up?
faq.a: The light is turned twice, once at the top and once at the bottom, and the two turns cancel out, so the image is upright and not swapped left to right.
asks: Is the periscope image upside down?

faq.q: What has replaced periscopes on modern submarines?
faq.a: Many new submarines use photonic masts: cameras and sensors on a mast that send pictures to screens. They need no viewing tube through the hull.

facts: A flat mirror at 45 degrees turns light through 90 degrees.
The US Navy's Virginia-class submarines use photonic masts instead of traditional periscopes.
Simple two-mirror periscopes are used to see over crowds and walls.
